text: This is the capstone: one real custom scoped application, built end to end across the next four lessons. The requirement — IT hands out laptops, monitors, and badges, and right now the only record is a spreadsheet that's always out of date.

Four actors, one workflow. The employee requests a specific item with a needed-by date. Their manager approves or rejects it before anything is fulfilled. IT then fulfills the approved request, checks the item out, and later marks it returned. And the platform itself flags anything overdue automatically, once the due date passes — the same kind of time-driven check Lesson 32 covered with scheduled scripts.

Before locking in any design, it's worth checking reality. This background script queries sc_task for short descriptions mentioning laptop or monitor, to see whether equipment-related data is already hiding somewhere else in the instance. Finding zero matches confirms there's no legacy data to migrate — this is a clean build.

Does this need its own application scope? Chapter 5 already answered this in the abstract. Lesson 19 showed that Global is one flat namespace where generic table names collide, and this requirement's table names — request, equipment — are exactly that generic. Nothing outside this feature needs direct access either, so the call is easy: this capstone lives in its own scope, x_acme_eqchk, created the same way Lesson 20 walked through.

The requirement itself already implies two tables. A request table carrying the approval state, who requested it, who approved it, and the due, checkout, and return dates — and because it needs that approval workflow, it extends task rather than starting from a bare custom table, inheriting state, assigned_to, and opened_by for free. And a separate equipment lookup table — the actual inventory data the request table will reference.
Requirements captured, scope decided, and the two tables sketched. Next up: actually building that data model, plus a real ACL that locks down who can edit the equipment's condition field.
